extracted.intended_audience: historians, students, and general readers interested in the history of advertising and historic print notices
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and features that make early printed advertisements effective, curious, eccentric, or notable — as evidenced by historical examples (blunders, puffery, event notices, classifieds, etc.). Useful for analysing or recreating period print ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives to curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements that deliberately provoke curiosity or puzzle the reader (e.g., melodramas, rebuses, mysterious phrasing) to draw attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes 'incentives to curiosity' such as 'melodramas, and puzzling as rebuses.' These devices are treated as a deliberate class of attention-getters that will be discussed further; examples throughout include odd phrasing and sensational claims designed to make readers want more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of compositional blunders (grammar and phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads should observe the rules of English composition; slips and grammatical mistakes often make notices unintentionally comical or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text groups many specimens whose 'comicality is mainly dependent upon sins against the rules of English composition.' Examples: 'a keyless lady's gold watch', 'a spinster particularly fond of children ... wishes for two or three having none of her own.' Such errors change meaning and public reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of modifiers and avoidance of ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrasing must avoid ambiguous modifiers that create double meanings (e.g., who or what the adjective applies to).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by 'an accomplished poodle nurse. Wages £1 per week.' The ad is ambiguous: is it a nurse for accomplished poodles, or an accomplished nurse? Ambiguity can be comic but may frustrate the advertiser's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puffery and extravagant hyperbole to promote events
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical and event advertising often employs extreme praise and hyperbolic language (puffery) to create buzz and fill houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter reproduces an effusion about Sarah Siddons ('this comet of the stage! this sun of the firmament of the Muses!... one hundred and nine ladies fainted!') as an example of advertising/puffery that likely helped draw audiences despite its excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of social/financial particulars in vital notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Obituaries and marriage announcements commonly included social details and sums (estates, fortunes) that signalled status and attracted reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical notices often gave the amount a person 'died worth' or the sums 'obtained with the brides' — e.g., marriages listing 'a beautiful lady of 50,000l. fortune.' The book notes the change and prominence of such particulars in early newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of free printed matter as promotional tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributing gratis printed pamphlets, lists, or small books to attract customers or prepare audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the New Masquerade Warehouse ... are given gratis PRINTED Speeches, Jokes, Jests, Conundrums...' — showing that giving away printed material was an established advertising stratagem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear operational details and liability/terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Service and transport advertisements should state schedules, fares, handling of parcels, and liability limits to set customer expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from a coach/diligence ad: schedules (days/times), fare ('Fare from Bristol to Swansea 1l. 10s., passage included') and an express condition: 'no parcels will be accounted for above 5l. value, unless entered as such and paid for accordingly.' Clear terms reduce disputes and define service scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and partnership notices: explicit instructions for creditors/debtors
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements of partnership dissolution or business changes should clearly instruct those indebted or claiming accounts where to send or pay them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dissolution notice between Robert and Thomas Southey telling 'all persons to whom the said partnership stood indebted, are to send their accounts to Robert Southey ... and the persons indebted to them, are respectfully requested to pay the same to the said Robert Southey.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Event invitations and rural festival adverts: list attractions/prizes and use engaging copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Public festival or bridal invitations succeeded when they listed entertainments, races, prizes and employed convivial or poetic language to attract attendance and contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple 'BRIDEWAIN'/'PUBLIC BRIDAL' adverts use verses, lists of 'races for prizes' (saddle, bridle, hunting horn), and promises of 'wrestling, and fencing and dancing' to entice wide attendance and donations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading to prevent printer's errors and unintended meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful proofreading is essential because typographical/printer's errors can change sense and provoke unintended responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book recounts a printer's error that turned an ad into 'a gent,' which inundated the advertiser with applications and personal attentions — showing how misprints can have real consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of owner/contextual description for novelty or persuasive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing an item's owner or provenance (often with whimsical detail) can create intrigue or perceived value in sale notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'about six dozen of prime port wine, late the property of a gentleman forty years of age, full in the body and with a high bouquet.' Or 'Erard grand piano, the property of a lady, about to travel in a walnut wood case with carved legs.' Such contexts add color and selling points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and register: avoid pompous, obscure formal language when clarity is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Legalistic or overly ornate phrasing in public notices can make the meaning obscure or comic; clarity of purpose should guide register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book reproduces a clumsy formal notice ('a Multiplicity of Dangers are often incurred by Damage of outrageous Accidents by Fire...') as an example where grandiose wording undermines clarity and invites ridicule.
